subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The people will find out that the increases under the minister's regime are considerably higher than our proposed increases. I do not want to touch on this subject too much, but the budget deficit is a matter of no account to the NDP because they do not care about deficits. They have never had anything but deficits in their lives and they do not care if the country is deficit-ridden. The deficit matters because the ever-increasing deficit makes it pretty well impossible to overcome inflation.
If hon. members do not believe me, then I suggest they ask governor Bouey. My authority is governor Bouey and hundreds of other economists. The Minister of Finance is now heart-to-heart, step-to-step and toe-to-toe-and I will not say anything else that he is-with the governor of the Bank of Canada. If he listens to the governor, he will understand why his burgeoning deficit is inflationary. The deficit has gone up to over $14 billion. It is up $3.6 billion from what it would have been under our government. Perhaps our deficit might have gone up-I will concede that-by a few hundred million dollars because the economic turndown is more extensive than we had prophesied. So our deficit might have been up a little bit. It
could have been that my confrere at the desk here could not have held down expenditures because we would have lost some revenues. It might have been up, but it would not have been up by $3.6 billion.
What difference does it make? The money has to be borrowed. The government gets some of it from government civil servants who pay into pensions. The government uses that money-borrows it. If I were a government civil servant I would be concerned about the money I am paying into these pension funds because the value of money is steadily declining. Anyway, the government gets its hands on this. In addition to the couple of billion dollars it will be able to use this year from those sources, the government has to go to our financial markets to borrow money-in excess of $12 billion this year, and a huge figure next year and the year after. This means they are going out to compete with the private sector and everyone else who wants to borrow.
Unless the governor of the Bank of Canada increases the money supply, interest rates will go up, because the demand is going to be greater than the supply. Interest rates will have a tendency to go up unless the governor of the Bank of Canada prints more money. The governor of the Bank of Canada says it is wrong to print more money. He says we have to keep the increase in the money supply down to correspond better with the increase in what we produced. But we are not producing more, Mr. Speaker; instead, we have a one per cent decline in GNP this year.
In any event, the governor of the Bank of Canada is going to have to say, "No, I cannot increase the money supply just because you will not listen to me. Just because you will not help me with your fiscal policies to fight inflation, I am not going to increase the money supply. There is no real value in my increasing the money supply." He is going to say, "We did that years earlier, in the first half of the 1970s, and we have changed our policy. We are not going to do it again." That is what he will say and I hope he will stick to it.
This means that interest rates will have to go up, Mr. Speaker, because the government is out there borrowing and taking the room of the private sector. That is why the deficit is inflationary. Why is it inflationary? It is inflationary because it discourages the private sector from investing and building and expanding. Why should they do these things when they have a government that is intervening in all their actions, a government that does not care about whether they make any kind of profit or not, a government that is going to sic FIRA on them and extend this great bureaucracy of FIRA so that it can come into their business if they are foreign-owned or have any element of that at all and peer over their shoulders and tell them what to do. That is why we have to be concerned about the deficit.
Why else do we have to be concerned about the deficit, Mr. Speaker? Because this year $10,250 million is to be spent on interest payments. I am now addressing the taxpayers of Canada, from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria, British
October 29, 1980

Columbia. The trouble with Canada is that part in between! 1 am addressing these taxpayers, Mr. Speaker, and telling them that one out of every four of their tax dollars is earmarked to pay interest on the government's debt this year. That is a stupendous figure. Next year, interest costs will amount to $12,265 million; in excess of 16 per cent of all government expenditures this year and next year are going to pay interest on the debt. That is the present estimate. It is a huge amount of money.
Do taxpayers wonder why they cannot have new services from the government? Do they wonder why they cannot have better transportation in Newfoundland? Do the fishermen wonder about small crafts and harbours and why they cannot get their harbours and wharves looked after? It is because the Minister of Finance has this huge bill for interest on past debts and it is going to get larger next year. The estimates show that it will go up by a couple of billion dollars every year.
The only way to get that under control, Mr. Speaker, is to reduce the amount being borrowed. It should be remembered, too, that over the last eight years, from 1972 to 1980, this government reduced taxation on every occasion before an election. The amount of those tax reductions this year totals altogether $9 billion-there is another $7.5 billion due to indexing, but this has nothing to do with indexing. I am dealing with tax cuts. There is $9 billion in tax cuts. For example, in November, 1978, the Minister of Justice then the minister of finance, brought in his budget and reduced the sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent which will cost $1,100 million this year.
If the government says it needs more revenue-and the government is not finished yet, because the minister is going to have to get more revenue before he is through-taxpayers should remember that the government fooled them in the last eight years by pretending that they did not need revenue. Going into elections, they pretended that they did not need the $9 billion from the taxpayers of Canada. Now they are safely back in office and ensconced on their voyage for another four years, they are going to start getting that revenue back. We can be sure of that. There will be a bigger revenue grab than has been announced in this budget before the next four years are over. This is why, Mr. Speaker. The deficits for the last eight years total $49,679 million and if we add to that this year's deficit of $14,150 million, there is a total for the eight years, including this one, of $63,829 million in deficits.
I know the government does not worry about deficits because they are not expecting to be here when the final bills come in for payment. I can tell you, however, Mr. Speaker, that this is a grim record. If we look at what the situation was before we got into this mess, when the Prime Minister first wended his weary way off the diving boards into office, we will see what happened. I think I have some of the figures here. At that time, in 1968-69 I believe, the bill for interest was about $1 billion. Now it is the figure that I have already given.
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
I have so many notes, Mr. Speaker, that I do not know whether I can find a particular note right away or not. But I have great faith that I will, if you will just put up with me. Here is another little note that I found while looking for the first note. Canada is $75 billion in debt to the rest of the world. This is the government that is telling off the rest of the world-telling them "get off the globe". What is that song about the world-"Stop the world, we want to get off!" This government is saying to foreign investors, "You come to Canada, gentlemen, and we are going to have our hands not only in your pockets but somewhere else even worse." That is what they are saying to foreign investors. They are very independent. They have this ersatz Canadian nationalism policy that they want to pretend will not cost anybody anything. But they owe the rest of the world $75 billion. That is what Canada owes the rest of the world and this year the amount is going up. The current account deficit for this year is estimated by the Minister of Finance at $6.2 billion, for last year it was $5.8 billion and the forecast for 1981 is $5.5 billion. So much for the services of these gentlemen! When the people who are owed that money decide to take a stand-look out. They will not be long in changing the minds of this government.
I knew I would find my note, Mr. Speaker. Here it is. There have been two budgets that showed a surplus since the Hon. Douglas Abbott was minister of finance in the early 1950s. There have been two budgets with a surplus out of the last 31 budgets. Mr. Douglas Abbott was minister of finance at the time of the last surplus. From Sir John A. Macdonald to Lester B. Pearson, from confederation to centennial year, the combined budgetary deficits of the federal government totalled $17 billion. With the present budget, the net debt of the government will be over $81 billion by next March. All of that increase is a gift to us from the Prime Minister. He is bequeathing us the difference between $17 billion and $81 billion. The gross debt of the federal government in 1967 was $30 billion; by next March it will be about $122 billion. This is the great legacy of the Trudeau years. In addition to the strain he is putting on the whole confederation now in attempting to mould it in his own fanatical way, this is another part of what he is bequeathing to Canada.
When he ascended his throne in 1968 interest charges on the national debt were $1.2 billion; we know what they are this year and next year the figure will be in excess of $12 billion.
I could give other startling and alarming figures, Mr. Speaker, but I do not want to startle and alarm the hon. gentlemen opposite too much. They might wake from their lethargy.
On page 35 of the budget document a lot of other deficits and borrowings are shown that are not included in the government's deficit. Under the heading "Loans, Investments and Advances" there appears the following statement:
In 1980-81 direct market borrowings by agent Crown corporations are expected to increase by a further $1.6 billion, resulting from borrowings by Export Development Corporation- $802 million; Eldorado Nuclear- $80 million, and the Federal Business Development Bank- $755 million, partially offset by repayments of $40 million by Petro-Canada.

October 29, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
That is a fine gesture. Petro-Canada's part is to repay $40 million while oil and gas consumers are asked to pay billions. There it is, Mr. Speaker-another $1.6 billion that the agent Crown corporations are borrowing in 1980-81. This can be added to the government debt because every dollar of the debt of those agent Crown corporations is a debt of the Government of Canada, if any one of them goes belly up.
I just heard a grunt over there in the NDP ranks. They do not agree. They do not agree with anything in the NDP. It is $1.6 billion. They do not like to hear any talk of debts. The hon. member from Winnipeg Birds Nest is getting all stirred up. So there is another $ 1.6 billion.
Let us pass on from the deficit because it annoys members of the NDP, the little red rump of the Liberal party. I am almost missing points, and they are important points.
I refer now to page 13. Here is what the Minister of Finance speaking for the government promised to do about expenditures. Just listen to this. Hear ye, hear ye! All ten provincial governments please pay attention to this:
A large element of our expenditures especially in the social affairs envelope consists of transfers to the provincial governments. 1 have already indicated to my provincial colleagues that we will be examining these programs closely as they come up for renewal, and we expect to achieve significant savings here.
Where does this government say it is going to get significant savings from the programs it induced the provinces to enter into in the social service field? It is presumably in Medicare, the Canada welfare plan, hospital insurance and Canada assistance. They are going to put the squeeze on the ten provinces to achieve it. There is no expenditure reduction in these estimates. There is a tremendous burgeoning of expenditures. Where are they going to get some of that money? They are going to squeeze it out of the ten provinces. These ten provinces are supposed to be supermen. We are led to believe that these ten have ganged up on the Prime Minister. As I said the other day, "little granny Trudeau with these ten big brutes, get him in a room and assault him". That is the picture we are given. It is the wrong picture. It is superman Trudeau and the ten midgets. That is the real picture, because the ten provinces have no powers compared to the power of the central government. It is the biggest canard of the century that the federal government is weak or that the federal government does not have power. It has overwhelming power and the government is going to use those overwhelming powers now to squeeze those ten provincial governments. The budget document reads: "We expect to achieve significant savings here". That means the provinces, including the poorest provinces such as my own province of Newfoundland, and the province of Prince Edward Island. All the provinces are going to have to pick up where this government reduces its spending. That is what this government is going to do. It will reduce its spending, even if it does so on the backs of the ten provincial governments. That is this government's great principle of equalization and the great principle of the Prime Minister and how he is going to help strengthen the regions of this country. The man is destroying
the regions of this country. He is destroying the country with it.
So this is what the minister promises. This is where he is going to achieve his expenditure reductions. This is the government that inveigled them into it and dangled the bait which they could not refuse politically. It gets them in, keeps them there for years and then gives it to them with significant expenditure reductions for the federal government.
Look at this sick joke on page 13:
I would like to announce at this time a special allocation of $350 million over four years-
Over four years!
-to promote industrial restructuring and manpower retraining and mobility in areas of particular need.
The total amount has been divided equally between economic development and social affairs envelopes. This sum of $350 million over four years-is that $85 million a year? Is it $85 million out of $60 billion this year? Is it $85 million out of $66 billion next year? There is going to be an additional $85 million for manpower, industrial restructuring and manpower retraining. That is called a program? That is not a program. That is not even an excuse for a program. In our budget we had $250 million for youth. This was an employment tax credit for youth alone which was a $150 million increase over what the previous government had. This is supposed to be a great program. It should not have even been in the budget as a footnote. It is an insult to even have that.
There is one other thing I need to refer to under this section. I ask hon. members not to get your hopes up. When I run out of new material, I will sit down, but there is a lot of material here. At page 33 having to do with equalization and fiscal transfers, it reads:
The equalization figures for 1980-81 and 1981-82 assume the passage of Bill C-24 now before Parliament.
The government is assuming that the bill will pass. It is the bill which takes Ontario out of the equalization formula. It will remove hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue which Ontario could have had if the changes had not been made. It is the bill that embodies the PUITTA changes. This assumes that it will pass the House, and the government has therefore reduced its expenditures by that amount.
By the way, anyone who believes that equalization is entrenched in the constitution had better take another look at the document before they continue to think that.
I mentioned unemployment insurance last night. There is an increase there. Let us look at my budget from last year. I want to share it with you. Let us have just one more brief mention of last year's budget with a certain fondness and tender regard. Let us look at page 18 of my budget and at page 17 of the government's budget for this year. What did we do in our budget last year? We explained employment programs and unemployment insurance. At page 18 of the 1979 budget, it reads:
October 29, 1980

The weekly employee rate of unemployment insurance contributions for 1980 will be increased from $1.35 per $100 of insurable earnings to $1.60. The employer rate will be increased from $1.89 to $2.24.
The howl from the hon. gentlemen then in the opposition was deafening. They said that this was unconscionable. They said it was another unconscionable thing that we should attempt to raise the contributions from employers and employees to help meet the heavy costs of unemployment.
What is in the budget for this year? At page 17, the Minister of Finance said this:
I am announcing on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, that effective January 1, 1981, the weekly rate of unemployment insurance contributions will be raised to $1.80 per $100 of insurable earnings. The employer rate of contribution will be increased to $2.52.
That is 20 cents more than we proposed. The employer rate of contribution will be increased to $2.52. We suggested $2.24. That is 28 cents more. These are very significant increases in both categories in excess of $1 billion this year. That will be taken from employers and employees by the government which last year decried the practice and wept crocodile tears on the floor of this House. There are a few similarities in these two budgets, except that the minister's budget was far more unconscionable than mine when it came to raising revenue.
Other speakers on our side will be dealing with questions such as of research and development and how that has been ignored, as far as we can tell, and how the economic development envelope has been increased. We are told the economic development envelope is supposed to include a western development fund of $4 billion. I assume it will have to be increased if it is going to include that. It is very hard to see what will be increased in the economic development envelope if there is to be an additional $4 billion for the west.
Let me suggest something to hon. gentlemen opposite. Instead of creating this $4 billion fund for the west, so-called, why do you not let the west look after their own development by treating them fairly and squarely with respect to oil and gas? The federal government has certain responsibilities in the west just as it has in the east and in the centre. It has the responsibility for giving them a decent transportation system, a decent system of ports and a decent system of shipping grain, all these things that we have a right to expect everywhere in Canada. There is no need for a special suggestion that there is going to be a $4 billion fund. This is conscience money.
They are thrashing the west. They are bearing down on the west. They are taking control over the oil and gas industry. They are taking away many of their ownership rights. Then they say: gentlemen, we are going to give you a $4 billion fund for western development which we are going to spend on your behalf. It just so happens that westerners would like to have their own $4 billion to spend in accordance with their own priorities. Let the federal government spend its own money, got legitimately in its proper, legitimate areas of policy across Canada in its own jurisdiction. Do not think westerners will thank you for that $4 billion development fund for the west, not at all.
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government should be leaving $4 billion with the west in its oil and gas regime and energy package. That is something it should be doing for the west, letting them develop themselves, not taking billions and billions from them and then giving them back a little. That is the same situation they want for Newfoundland.
Imagine the Minister of Justice threatening the premier of Newfoundland in this House last week. What is this country coming to when the big $60 billion Government of Canada says that a premier of this country cannot speak his mind on constitutional issues or he is going to suffer, the Government of Canada is not going to give him any assistance if he does not do what he is told-he will get nothing on the Lower Churchill if he does not watch what he says?
Why is it that hon. gentlemen opposite will not recognize the coastal provinces as being the owners of offshore minerals? Why? Because it wants us down there like trained seals, waiting for them to hand us our gifts just like they are now asking the west to put their paws out for $4 billion for a western development fund.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are not coming to Ottawa cap in hand to this government or anyone else in Ottawa, those of us from Newfoundland or in any of the maritime provinces. We are going to speak our minds. We are full citizens of Canada. We have been here 31 years and we are going to have our say with no threats or bullying by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). They are not going to deter our government, you can depend on that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Page 15 is where the minister is so satisfied with the capital gains tax. He is going to release a discussion paper.
It shows that Canada's system of taxing gains is favourable to taxpayers.
How come? Are they not paying any taxes at all? Is the minister going to index the capital gains tax? In all justice, if he is indexing the personal income tax as he should, there is a strong case for the capital gains tax to be indexed. Otherwise he is taxing the families of the poor farmer who dies. He is taxing them on all the inflationary elements of their so-called capital gains tax. The minister does not care about the inflation impact on capital gains. He says it is very favourable to the taxpayer. He said, and 1 quote:
As well, the taxes on inheritances and wealth in Canada are the lowest among 21 OECD countries surveyed. The paper notes that, while the system has imperfections, the taxation of capital gains is an important source of government revenue, has important lax structure implications and is essential for the equity and fairness of the system.
I wonder what the farmers are going to think of his position on capital gains and what the business sector is going to think. Much of their profit these days is not profit at all. It is because

October 29, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
of the effect inflation has on the revenues and their balance sheets, and they are taxed on that. I hope the minister will take a deeper look at the question of capital gains tax and business taxation generally.
I went into housing assistance last night. I will not go into it again. Because I want to have this mentioned in the main body of my address, let me just point out there is nothing for the home owner, nothing for the tenant, no shelter allowance, no mortgage interest and property tax relief. There is not one iota of help for people now buying homes who are paying rates of 15'A and 16 per cent. There is not one element of help for them.
Apparently these people do not deserve help anymore. Why not? Because the Liberal party is in government. They deserved help when the Liberal party was out of government, but they do not deserve it today when the Liberal party is in government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is only the MURB. This year the MURB is going to cost the government $15 million. The MURB will be some help in having a few more multiple unit residential dwellings built, but essentially it is a tax relief. It is a tax device which assists those with higher incomes while incidentally helping to build a few more housing units.
Why did 1 stop it last year? 1 stopped it because of advice from the Department of Linance. What was the advice? That MURBs are no longer needed. The advice was that the provinces are responsible for housing, property and civil rights and many of the provinces have policies that interfere with and do not give incentive to the building of housing units. Some of them have strict rent controls. They are discouraging investment in housing, apartments and the like. All this MURB business is doing is trying to offset things which the provinces are doing that they should not be doing to give disincentives for housing.
If the Department of Linance gave me that advice ten months ago, how can they now be giving different advice to this minister? The answer is, they cannot be. What is the answer? The answer is this. The minister said to his department, "Gentlemen, there is nothing in this budget for housing. There is no assistance for housing. I have to have something, no matter how tattered. 1 need to have something to put in for housing so that I can pretend 1 am concerned about the housing situation in Canada."
We have had the lowest number of housing starts year after year for the last four or five years. 1 believe this is the worst year ever. Is that correct?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you. Therefore, the minister came up with a MURB. Resurrect the MURB. If anything needed to be resurrected, that was not one of the most important. The MURB might help this year. It might attract certain wealthy Canadians to put some money into building apartment units
and condominiums in certain areas of the country. Lor example, it will be very useful in British Columbia. There is a strong demand there for the MURB.
It is not even a flea bite in dealing with the housing problem, with the people who occupy houses or who are tenants in this country today. Where we were going to give the home owners this year $575 million in assistance, what are they offering the home industry? They are offering a $15 million deduction in revenue for MURB. Where we were going to give $1.2 billion next year to help the home owners of this country, they are going to give $15 million in MURBs. Enough said. I won't go into that.
I will give just one quotation because I am sick of showing what was said by members opposite when they were in opposition as compared to what they are doing now. One more little plank in the coffin. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in the House of Commons on November 19, 1979, said:
The government could have started where the real problem lies and could have provided something for rental assistance.
Did the Minister of Employment and Immigration, once he was in power, go to the Minister of Finance and say that the real problem is there and something should be provided for rental assistance? He spent all his time in the couple of brief months in opposition saying that to us, that what was needed was assistance for the renters in Canada. Now this minister has not done anything.
There are a lot of other areas I could cover. I suppose we do want the members of the New Democratic Party to get on today so that they can move their subamendment. They are so good at subamendments. Their last subamendment-what an excuse for an opposition party that was over begging the government for favours.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), just like a trained seal, went over begging for a scrap from the Prime Minister. He says: "Give me a scrap. Give me a scrap to help me in my problem. I have dissidents in my caucus. My caucus is all westerners except for a little, tiny pink rump here in Ontario. The Ontario rump is three people and the western rump is a big, healthy, steak-like rump. I have a dispute in my caucus and the western people in my caucus are very, very agitated about what you are doing in the energy field. They do not like this constitutional package and I have got to try to get them quietened down because I am from Ontario, from a district in Ontario. I am seriously worried that my position is going to be in jeopardy in the next election. Please help me, Prime Minister. What can you do to help?" That was the Leader of the NDP in his conspirators' meeting with the Prime Minister a week or ten days ago. And the Prime Minister said: "Don't worry about this, Ed. I offered to take you in with me after the election, you refused me, nevertheless, I, in my wisdom, am going to help you, Ed. I am going to give the right of indirect taxation to Saskatchewan and I am going to pretend that I am going to help you in the resource area, when
October 29, 1980

really I am only endangering the whole resource structure for the ten provinces across Canada." So, Mr. Broadbent threw in the hat. When he threw in the hat he threw in Mr. Nystrom with it. He went with the hat.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Their last subamendment destroyed a budget that was going to help Canada in the short term and the long term. It was going to help the medium and lower-income people of Canada. I demonstrated that earlier today. They are so blind in their NDP fanaticism that they destroyed a budget which would have helped the people they say they represent. Now they do not represent them one iota more than 1 do and they have not got any more of a heart than I have got. But I do not go around every day beating my gums about the great heart I have got. I do not wear it on my sleeve like the NDP.
Why do we in this party want to help the Canadian economy? Why is it we seem to have a fixation with the economy and producing more and more? Why? Because that is the only way we can give the people of Canada who need more, more. You cannot give them more if the pie is shrinking and not expanding. That is why we are concerned with the economy. So if we do not wear our hearts on our sleeve like the NDP it is not because we are not thinking of the little people of this country. The little people of this country are not going to have a thing if the economy of this country goes on for the next four or five years as it has gone on over the last four or five. There will be nothing for those people and we will be in a mad fight because the pie does not grow, it is diminishing. The groups who are suffering will be fighting one another for a piece of the pie and the people who are going to get the pie are the organized sections of society; the senior citizens are not going to get it. The defenceless and the unorganized are not going to get a piece of the pie. That is why we are concerned about the economy. That is why we wanted to take a long-term look, because if we do not take a long-term look there is going to be nothing for anyone. That is why we are concerned.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
That is why I am hoping, with the moving of this motion, that we are going to destroy this government next Tuesday. Do not laugh, there may be 30 or 40 statesmen on the other side-there might be. After all, I was a statesman myself once and a member of the Liberal party and I left it. There may be 20 or 30 over there who will take the step to
The Budget-Mr. Rae
save Canada next Tuesday by voting for this motion. That is why I have couched it in extremely diplomatic terms, with the assistance of our House leader. So, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This House condemns the government for the regressive nature of its budget and rejects the budget because it fails to assist monetary policy to combat inflation, fails to meet the campaign commitments of the Prime Minister, fails to control government spending, fails to reduce unemployment, fails to help low or middle-income Canadians meet increasing living costs, fails to advance effective policies to achieve oil self-sufficiency and fails to maintain national unity".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, after that exercise in primal therapy I thought I would concentrate on this year's budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a Liberal budget. I think it was Woody Guthrie who said that some rob you with a six-gun and some with a fountain pen. If the Canadian public was held up by the budget last year there is little question it is being held up by the budget this year. The techniques are different. I do not agree with those people who say there is no difference between the Conservative party and the Liberal party. There is a difference of style. There is some difference of substance.
This is a budget which in its own way is just as unacceptable, just as harsh, just as regressive and just as reactionary as the one which was rejected not only by the NDP last year- surely the member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) could hardly have expected us to support his budget- not simply by the Liberal party united strangely in the thought they could win power. I would remind those members of the Conservative party, who continue to return to those halcyon days prior to February, that between the defeat of the budget and the return of the Liberal government there was an event of some significance. That event was an election.
If you want to take your case to anybody, in terms of blaming them for what happened, I suggest to those members of the Conservative party that they take their case once again to the Canadian people. There are to those who say, "Well, the NDP can hardly be expected to criticize the economic policies of the Liberal party because they were opposed to the economic policies of the Conservative party." I have heard comments such as that. It is a strange and wonderous thing that a person can be opposed to cholera in 1979 and be opposed to leprosy in 1980.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a strange and wonderous thing that we can attack one party of government for following policies which inflict great hardship on Canadian people and provide no economic leadership, and once again when another party takes power we can be just as critical of that same party for following exactly the same trend and the same thrust of policies. In fact, far from it being an inconsistency it is the

October 29, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Rae
height of consistency and, I think, the height of a commitment to a certain number of principles which I hope to outline.
In my view this budget represents the three Ds of Liberalism. This budget is profoundly disappointing. It represents an opportunity missed. This budget is duplicitous. This budget, most important, is damaging to the Canadian economy, to the Canadian worker and to the future of our country.
In terms of our disappointment, I think all of us as members of Parliament should focus not simply on the balance sheet which has been presented, not simply on what is there and not simply on the number of issues which were raised by the hon. member for St. John's West but perhaps most clearly on our own constituencies and constituents. We should be thinking of the people who day in and day out work in those constituencies, cities and communities. When we return to our ridings on weekends or whenever we can to meet with our constituents, we should think of what it is that strikes at the hearts of those people. The thing which struck me about this budget is that just as in the other budget there was no mention of the unemployed. There was mention of unemployment. We have projections of what it will be this year, next year and the year after. Incidentally, it will be higher this year than it was last year and it will be over one million in the five years to come.
That is the kind of projection we are getting from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), but I am not speaking about unemployment as a concept or idea. I am speaking of and thinking of the unemployed. As I am sure many hon. members do, I am thinking of young people, old people, not so young people, not so old people and the men and women who come in constantly and say, "Mr. Rae"-or whoever, Mr. Rose or Mr. Nystrom-"I would like you to help me find a job". We must constantly respond, if we are not members of the government party, if we are not living in that part of the world where patronage is a way of life, as is my case in the city of Toronto, by referring people to Manpower or trying to get them interviews or seeing if we can do something through the manpower system. But basically the force which dictates the level of unemployment and the fate of unemployed people is not whether the individual member of Parliament can make a telephone call and get somebody a job. It is whether or not there is a government in Ottawa which demonstrates leadership. I define leadership quite simply as an ability to respond to the deepest anxieties of the people, and ability to respond with compassion and direction and an ability to respond in a way which gives hope and strength to the Canadian people.
One thinks of a government like that of Roosevelt in 1932. One thinks of the Labour government in Britain in 1945. One thinks of those governments which decided they could change some things and some circumstances. They could tell people in certain situations that unemployment was not like the weather and not a function of climate but that unemployment was something which could be affected by the policies of government. We have never had such a government in this country. We have never had a "New Deal". We have never had a democratic socialist government. We have had the policies of
Mackenzie King, the policies of Mr. Trudeau, the policies of R. B. Bennett. We have had policies which have consistently told unemployed people that there was nothing which could be done. That is a very old message and basically a very mean message, a message of intellectual bankruptcy and precisely the message which is contained in the budget which has been put forward by the Minister of Finance. On September 9 in Halifax when the minister was making one of his few public speeches prior to the budget he said that a budget is more than a statement of economic accounts and more than a statement of how much we will spend and how much we will tax. "A budget must be an accounting of commitments, a statement of priorities and a blueprint for achieving our goals".
Measured by that very test which the Minister of Finance set out for us six short weeks ago, this budget is a failure. It is not an accounting of commitments. It is not a statement of priorities, and it is certainly not a blueprint for achieving our goals. Instead, the minister has made fun, as he is wont to do, of our party for talking about serious commitment. We asked him to make certain serious commitments, and he in his own way perhaps correctly said, "We in our party do not take ourselves quite so seriously. We are not in the habit of making serious commitments". The minister is in the habit of giving us lugubrious evasion, and I think what is represented in the budget today is lugubrious evasion. It fails to respond to the need for economic insecurity which racks so many of our communities. It fails to respond to unemployment levels in central, eastern and Atlantic Canada which are unacceptable. It fails to recognize the fact that Canada now has, has had for some time and will continue to have under this government, because of its projections and because of the policies it is making, the highest level of unemployment in the industrial world.
That is the only economic record in the OECD which we can claim to hold. We do not spend more than anybody else on research and development. We do not yet have the highest rate of inflation. We do not have the highest per capita income. We have one achievement and one achievement alone, and that is, we continue to have the highest rate of unemployment in the western world.
I am not going to refer to duplicity at the moment. Hon. members opposite said some things when in opposition and now say something else when in government. We have seen governments come and go and change a number of times in the past couple of years. Believe me, if we did not have a program we would not know who the players are. When the Tories are in opposition, they suddenly become the workers' friend. Mr. Crosbie suddenly portrays himself as a friend of the poor and disadvantaged. That is an unique role for him. In opposition we saw that Mr. Gray was the opponent of high interest rates. As Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When he was the hon. member for Windsor West and finance critic of the Liberal party, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray)-and I happened to be on the same television program-promised that he would resign if interest rates continued to rise, which they have done. They went down, and now they are going up again. However, that is not the principal point 1 want to make. The point I want to make is that there is a commitment and a consensus that unemployment will remain high. There is a consensus that inflation will remain high, and an examination of the budgets of the present Minister of Finance and the previous minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West, will indicate that that consensus exists and will continue to exist.
We can talk about a co-conspiracy. It is against that consensus that we in this party are speaking, and it is about the fact of unemployment and about the difficulties and the human cost of unemployment that we have to speak. 1 am constantly amazed that budgets can refer to unemployment statistics, but budgets can never mention the cost in human terms of being unemployed. Yet that is as much a reality as the statistics mentioned in the tables which are distributed with such glee and fervour by the Minister of Finance and his associates. We would have looked, for example, for a budget which recognized that because of the rates of inflation and unemployment there have been dramatic changes in our society.
There has been, for example, a dramatic loss in wages right across the country, with only two provinces being exceptions, a loss of wages of $200 on an average in the province of Ontario and $450 in the province of Newfoundland, nearly $1,200 a year. We have to deal with the fact that this very budget, rather than attempting to reverse the direction, attempting to establish a cost of living tax credit which would provide for advantages, for credits, and for income where income is needed most, the most progressive form of indexation that can be devised, the minister has continued with the old system of indexation which will guarantee that the average wage earner will fall further and further behind the cost of living.
We have to recognize that in this economy in the last year there have been 1,000 lay-offs a day. Every working day, 1,000 people are laid off right across Canada. One has to laugh rather than cry when one reads the response of the minister to this kind of situation. On page 13 of the budget he refers to the pension system which he describes, not as a disgrace or as
The Budget-Mr. Rae
tragedy for workers who have been laid off and left without pensions, not as something that affects the very justice of our system when workers in their fifties are laid off and are not able to find jobs, but as "defective in many ways". He describes the present pension system as "uneven". But then he has a final criticism. He says that not only is it uneven, it also hinders labour mobility. What about labour security, Mr. Speaker? What about the fundamental principle of economic rights, the rights in the constitution? What about the fundamental principle that, as well as being mobile, people also want to be secure? People also want the assurance, not that they have to move from Newfoundland, from Cape Breton or even from Toronto to go to Alberta in order to find a job, but that their government will be concerned to see that they get a job in the communities where they want to raise their families. That is the principle which is at stake when the minister talks about pensions and refers to the fact that there is no labour mobility.
The budget is a disappointment because it reads almost as if the minister had decided not to take so many critical decisions. For example, one reads the paragraph on the country's tax system and one wonders whether this is a statement by the Minister of Finance or a statement by a professor of economic theory talking about what kind of a budget it might be a good idea to bring in one day. This is what he has to say on page 15 of the budget. He observes that we have created a mammoth system, a grotesque system of tax expenditures, with tax expenditures now worth well over last year's figure of $32 billion. The minister says:
Tax incentives tend to pyramid with the result that a number of profitable corporations or wealthy individuals pay little or no tax.
The fact is that in 1978 there were 96 Canadians, and right now we know we have well over 100 Canadians, making over $200,000 a year who pay not a penny in tax, and the minister says this is what tends to happen. He tells us that other countries have responded by introducing minimum rates. He says:
While this approach may be an answer to the problem, perhaps a fundamentally different one would be preferable.
Is the minister going to tell us? I thought his job as Minister of Finance was to respond to the family making $15,000 a year which sees the inequity, which sees a stratum of people being subsidized by average taxpayers so they can spend their winters in Florida and their summers wherever they please. That is the system which the Minister of Finance is perpetrating and defending. He says:
One questions whether the economy might not be better served by a tax system with lower rates-
He says "one questions". What is this, an academic seminar? I would have thought the minister would have said not that "one questions" but that this is an abuse which has grown, that they recognize their mistakes, they see they were at fault and they are prepared now to do something about it. But that is not their response. Their response is that they question whether it might not be better for the economy. There is not a mention of social justice, not a mention of the disease of envy that is created in a society where you have such

October 29, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Rae
inequality. That does not feature in this budget. Those words are not trendy at the moment. It is not done to talk about equality in our society. It is all supply economics and what is good for the macro-economy, and it may not be good for the macro-economy to have so much money being sheltered from the tax system.
One can say the same for capital gains. The minister tells us he is looking forward to a good discussion on the problem of capital gains. There is no mention in this budget of the problem of equity. There is no mention in this document of an industrial strategy for our country. It is amazing that a government should have laboured so long and produced a document which says nothing about the problems of our industries. We have the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who is desperate for funds, who is faced with crises week after week. He comes to the House looking exhausted and worn out. He has been in negotiations giving away the sink to Chrysler Corporation and to Massey-Ferguson. He comes to the House desperately trying to explain what he has been doing. Is there a mention in this document of industrial strategy? Is there a mention in this document of the problems faced by central Canada, by Quebec and by Atlantic Canada? Is there a mention of runaway plants and workers left abandoned? They talk about spending $350 million over four years, $85 million a year. That is a lot of money these days, Mr. Speaker, and it will go far to deal with the problem of industrial restructuring. There is no mention of the underlying disease, no analysis of what is causing this problem, no mention of the fact that there are people in every industrial city in this country and in every community who are looking for leadership, who are looking to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to the Minister of Finance to show leadership, to show that just as much as they are prepared to take steps on the constitution, just as much as they are concerned with our becoming politically whole, so too are they concerned about the country becoming economically whole once again.
I can think of no greater condemnation of this government than that they have learned nothing in opposition, that they have seen nothing of what is demanded of Canadian people, and that they continue with a policy which lacks direction, which lacks compassion and which does not speak to the Canadian people in the language and in terms they can understand, in terms that will allay the anxieties which exist in far too many homes. I could mention the fact that this document says nothing about a science policy for Canada, the fact that scientists are leaving by the dozens and by the hundreds from our universities, the fact that we suffer now from an intellectual brain drain, that we have to constantly import scientists from overseas, the fact that there are fields of research and science into which our young people will not go any more because there is no hope, no industry, no determination for the government to say, "Yes, we have a technological policy, yes, we have a scientific policy, and we are prepared here to provide employment for people coming out of our universities."
This is a disappointing document because it is fundamentally empty. It is a duplicitous document because it is doing things it claims it is not doing and because it is not doing things which it claims to be doing. It is doing things it claims not to be doing; it is claiming that it is not increasing taxes. But what are unemployment insurance contributions if they are not a tax on payroll, if they are not a tax which comes out of the salary of every salaried employee and which comes out of the payroll of every employer who hires an employee? What are they, if not a labour cost for the employer just as much as if the employee paid for those costs himself? The minister understands what I am talking about. The minister knows perfectly well that the unemployment insurance contribution is a tax just as surely as any other form of tax. Also he knows that it is a regressive tax, and because of the upper limit of $15,000, he knows that the average working Canadian pays for his own unemployment. No one else pays, and they call that redistribution and equalization. It is redistribution among the working people of Canada. It is not redistribution from those who have to those who do not have. It is duplicitous because they are saying there is no tax and then they are imposing a tax, only they are doing it another way.
The hon. member for St. John's West did not mention one interesting contrast between his budget and that of the Minister of Finance. In the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West, they increased unemployment insurance contributions. That is true, but in their explanation they said, "We are increasing them from $1.30 to $1.60." Mr. Speaker, do you want to know what the minister said in this budget? He said, "We are increasing unemployment insurance contributions to $1.80." From where? Do the press know from where? Does the average citizen reading the budget know from where? Would it have taken anything other than a commitment to openness to say that they were raising them from such and such to such and such which represents a net increase of 33Vs per cent? That is all it would have required, yet it is symbolic. It is a small thing, it is not a major thing, but it is symbolic of this government that they will not even tell us in their own budget what the net increase is. Everyone must figure it out for himself.
This has got to be the height of chutzpah. They tell us there will not be a natural gas export tax. The minister said they received so much opposition from the producing provinces, Alberta and British Columbia, that they decided not to impose an export tax and as an alternative, which is the way the minister described it in his budget, he was proposing a very different kind of tax. He was not going to tax the export of gas, he was going to tax all gas. I see the minister nodding his head. I would simply say to him that what he proposed is not an alternative, it is an addition. I woke up to the CBC news on the radio this morning and heard the press solemnly saying, "There is no export tax on natural gas; the government has handed out an olive branch to the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia." It is not an olive branch. Who is the minister trying to kid? He is simply providing a natural gas
October 29, 1980

tax and in addition he will tax everybody else. That is all it is.
I think this should be said clearly. They are taxing the exports of natural gas, they are taxing domestic consumption of natural gas and all forms of natural gas.
I understand I need to move the subamendment in order to gain some extra time. I should like to move a subamendment to the amendment of the hon. member for St. John's West. 1 do not think any cannons will go off if I move it. Therefore, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
and this House condemns the government for continuing the Liberal-Conservative policies that have brought Canada to its most serious recession since 1954, in particular for its policies of high interest rates, indifference to the poor, punitive taxes, and inflated prices; and this House further condemns the government for its failure to introduce in this budget a program of capital investment, a fair prices commission, cost of living tax credits and a serious commitment to public ownership in the oil industry to ensure that Canadians would no longer be industrial tenants in their own land.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will leave the question of energy as the key example of the government not doing things it claims to be doing. I do not want to spend a great deal of time on this because of the limitations of time and because the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) will be dealing with this question, but I want to make clear to the minister the nature of our objection. 1 am glad the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is here. In the question period today 1 mentioned the cost to the Canadian economy of this phony goal of 50 per cent Canadian ownership. We are trading David Rockefeller for Conrad Black. So what? What is the importance of this?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Big deal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Big deal, as the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) said. The key point is that the outflow of dividends will continue to be as big a problem in 1990 as it is now. It will be even bigger, because the amounts we are talking about will be so much bigger than they are at the moment. It means that the multinationals will be allowed to increase their market share. It means a few wealthy Canadians will benefit from this phony nationalism and that there will be continued foreign domination and outflow of dividends. The goal of 50 per cent ownership is meaningless unless one talks about control. It is a meaningless figure, it is a meaningless idea. It is so meaningless that it was stated by the Prime Minister in 1974 as one of his key objectives of the next six years. In the national energy policy released last night the minister said, "We do not know how we will get there, we have no method of enforcing it, but it continues to be a very important objective of the government."
The hard fact of the matter is that we are charging $16.75 for a barrel of oil right now. Imperial Oil, the largest oil company in Canada, has total assets worth $4.6 billion and an annual revenue of $6.6 billion. The province of Manitoba has revenues of $1.7 billion. That is the size and kind of institution
The Budget-Mr. Rae
about which we are talking when we are charging $16.75 for a barrel of oil. Imagine what revenues will flow and what the assets side of Imperial Oil will be by 1990. Imagine how big, how mammoth it will be, all of it subsidized by the phony policy of this government.
It is just amazing the press is able to say that it represents a tremendous advance to Canadianization and that we in the NDP must be really worried because the Liberals are moving in on our ground. We were shaking in our boots last night as the minister read his statement. We felt that the two ministers combined had come up with a real radical document. Imperial Oil will only own all of Canada by 1990, and we can take satisfaction from the fact that 50 per cent of it will be owned by the wealthiest people in Canada! That gives us a lot of worry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a fake to the left.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) has so aptly described it, it is the biggest fake to the left since the last fake to the left of the Liberal party.
Finally, this is a profoundly damaging budget because it continues to apply the same unsuccessful phony remedies as have been applied by Liberal and Conservative governments to our basic economic problems for too long. It is damaging in another sense, because it is an admission of defeat. It is a declaration of intellectual bankruptcy because it does by stealth what the Tories tried to do openly, but it does exactly the same thing and has exactly the same effect.
1 should like to refer to just two matters because I know my colleagues will be referring to others.
The projections that are contained in this budget for the social services provided to the people of Canada by the Government of Canada indicate that those basic services will be under the most severe attack since they were established. There is no getting around that fact. There is no getting around the fact, for example, that the rate of growth in this so-called envelope will be 10.6 per cent in 1981, 6.3 per cent in 1982 and 6.9 per cent in 1983. I see that the minister would like to argue that this matter should be taken care of by the provinces. Will eight Tory provincial governments provide social services to the people of Canada? That is a statement coming from a government which is supposed to care about the provision of services for the people.
I say to the minister quite honestly, and I know his role personally in the introduction of medicare, that if this was the attitude of the Pearson government in the 1960s, we would never have had medical care for all Canadians; never. It is a guarantee that we will never take on the new challenge of providing daycare so that women can have a genuine choice between whether they want to stay at home and whether they want to go to work. We will never have a national co-ordinated system which guarantees that women in Newfoundland have the same rights in this vital field as the people of Manitoba or Saskatchewan. It is a guarantee that the over-all level of social

October 29, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Lalonde
spending and the provision of social services for all our people will go down.
That is not an abstraction. It means, quite simply, poorer people, more poorly clothed people, more poorly housed people, more poorly fed people and more poorly educated people. It is a tragic abdication of even the minister's professed interest in being progressive. I was reminded of the ultimate statement of bankruptcy when the minister said that the concept of sharing seems to be close to the distinctive fibre of the Canadian tradition, and that he does not think the state should do it all. What are we going to rely on, the United Way? Is that the answer, that we go back to the United Way and the handouts of lady dowagers who come down to the poor people of Broadview-Greenwood and say, "Here is a handout. I am sharing with you by bringing you a turkey at Christmas and a cake on your birthday."? Is that the kind of sharing about which the minister is talking?
The return to private charity is an abdication of the fundamental social rights of the Canadian people. The notion that we should return to some kind of private sharing is worthy of the rotarian that the Minister of Finance has now become.

Mr. Speaker, France had a socialist government 45 years ago. The premier of that government was a great socialist of democratic tradition, Leon Blum. At the end of his life someone asked him: Are you satisfied with what you have accomplished with your government, that popular government during the 1930s, those very difficult years? He replied: Well, yes, because 1 received a letter from a grandfather who wrote to me: "Thanks to you and to your government I was able to see the beach and the sea before dying."

There is not one Canadian, be he in Broadview-Greenwood, or be he anywhere else who will be able to write the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister and say, "As the result of this budget, thanks to you, 1 will finally be able to see the sea and the beach", because the seas and the beaches are reserved to exactly those people for whom they have been reserved for far too long in our society and nothing has been done to change that.
That is the simple reason why it gives me the greatest pride to move the amendment that 1 have moved to stand as firmly and as resolutely opposed to this phony budget, a mile wide and an inch deep, with its statement of intellectual bankruptcy and its condemnation of the Canadian people to a future far less bright, far less generous, far less hopeful and far less compassionate than the one they deserve.
